title: Max area of island
label: idb-list
statement:
A grid holds 0 (water) and 1 (land). An island is a group of 1s connected **horizontally or vertically**. Return the **area of the largest island**, or 0 if there is none.

*Note:* despite the name, this is **not** the twin of InterviewDB Q3 "Artificial island", which is a one-dimensional sliding window.
provenance: **InterviewDB-listed.** LeetCode 695 is on the LinkedIn list you supplied from InterviewDB. No candidate report of this exact question was found in the research passes — the evidence is that the list names it. On that list it is listed on its own, not tied to InterviewDB Q3. A name collision, not a match - check this before you revise it. 695 is 2-D flood fill over a grid. Q3 "Artificial Island" is a 1-D sliding window with a conversion budget. They share only the word *island*. The real public equivalent of Q3 is 1004 Max Consecutive Ones III, which is in the existing research as a reader-reported question.

stages.title: Largest island
stages.say: Return the area of the largest island of 1s in a grid.
stages.require: Implement `IslandArea.Max(grid)`. Islands are 4-connected (not diagonal). No island → 0. Do not change the grid; must survive a 1,000 × 1,000 island.

listen: Restates the problem and asks the clarifying questions that change the code (4-connected or 8-connected? (4.); May I mark the grid to save memory? (No — keep the caller's grid intac)
States the data structure, the invariant and the complexity before prompting
Reads AI output before running it

1.a: Marking on pop lets the same cell be pushed by up to four neighbours.

2.a: O(R × C) time and memory for the seen array.

3.q: Land cells arrive one at a time and you report the largest island after each.
3.a: Union-find with a size per root — LeetCode 305 / the "Number of clouds" question in this bank.

4.q: A grid too large for memory.
4.a: Process strips of rows, keeping union-find labels for the boundary row only.

5.a: InterviewDB Q3 "Artificial island" sounds like this but is a 1-D window over an array. Answering with a flood fill would be wrong.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- 4-connected or 8-connected? (4.)
- May I mark the grid to save memory? (No — keep the caller's grid intact.)
- Grid size? (Up to 1,000 × 1,000 — a recursive flood fill can overflow.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Scan every cell. Each unseen land cell starts a flood fill that counts the island's cells, marking them seen as they are pushed. Every cell is pushed at most once, so the whole scan is O(rows × cols).

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Recursive DFS overflowing on a big solid island.
- Marking cells seen when popped instead of when pushed, so a cell is pushed many times.
- Overwriting the input grid with 0s.
- Counting diagonal neighbours.
